### The Map in the Drawer

When the city decided to redraw its bus routes, Mara found an old map in the back of her kitchen drawer. It was folded into a square no bigger than her palm, its creases soft and white. The date in the corner was twenty-three years old. A coffee stain covered part of the river, and someone had written *ask about pears* beside the number 14 route.

She knew the handwriting was her father’s, though she could not remember what the note meant.

The new routes would begin on Monday. The number 14, which had run past her apartment since before she moved in, was being shortened. It would no longer cross the river or stop at the market. Mara had read the notices, attended a meeting, and signed a petition. None of it had changed the decision.

On Saturday morning, she took the old map and boarded the 14.

The driver was a woman Mara recognized but had never spoken to beyond greetings. A cardboard sign taped behind her seat said *LAST WEEKEND ON THIS ROUTE*. Someone had drawn a small, crooked heart beneath the words.

“Busy?” Mara asked as she paid.

“Busier than usual,” the driver said. “People keep telling me where they used to get off.”

Mara sat near the back. Outside, the city passed in the familiar sequence: pharmacy, laundromat, a narrow house with a stone lion on either side of its steps. She had traveled this road hundreds of times, usually looking at her phone or thinking about work. Today she watched for things that might have appeared on the old map.

At the fourth stop, an elderly man climbed aboard carrying a cake box. He held it level with both hands while the driver waited for him to sit.

“Birthday?” she called.

“Retirement,” he said.

“Congratulations!”

“I’m delivering it.”

The passengers laughed, and the man looked pleased, though he stared firmly at the box afterward.

Mara unfolded the map. Some streets had changed names. A public pool had become an apartment building; a train depot was now a food hall. The route still crossed the river at the same bridge, but the neighborhood beyond it had been colored yellow on the map and was gray in real life, its old warehouses converted to offices.

Her father had brought her to the market when she was a child. He bought tomatoes by pressing each one gently with his thumb, a habit that embarrassed her because it seemed to take so long. He also knew vendors by name, though Mara suspected he had learned most of those names by reading the signs above their stalls.

She remembered pears, too, but only after she saw the note. There had been a woman who sold them in paper bags, always adding one more after her father had paid. Perhaps he had wanted to ask whether they were in season. Or perhaps he had promised to bring some to a neighbor. The note seemed both intimate and unhelpful, like a message overheard through a wall.

Across the aisle, a boy was drawing the bus in a notebook. He had given it enormous wheels and a row of passengers whose heads floated above the windows.

“That’s good,” Mara said.

He showed her the page without smiling. “The wheels aren’t supposed to be that big.”

“I like them that way.”

His mother leaned over. “He’s been drawing buses all morning. His grandmother takes this one.”

“Not after today,” the boy said.

“She’ll take another one.”

“It’s not the same bus.”

His mother began to answer, then stopped. “No,” she said. “It isn’t.”

At the bridge, Mara pulled the cord. She had planned to go all the way to the market, but she wanted to walk the last part. The river looked lower than she remembered, exposing a strip of mud along the bank. A bicycle lay half-submerged near the reeds, its front wheel turning slightly in the current.

She crossed slowly. From the middle of the bridge, she could see both sides of the city: the older brick buildings behind her and the glass-fronted offices ahead. A man in running clothes passed her twice, once in each direction. On his second trip, he slowed to look at the bicycle.

“Think anyone’s coming back for it?” he asked.

“I doubt it,” Mara said.

He nodded and ran on.

The market was smaller than it had been in her childhood. Half the stalls now sold prepared lunches, and the flower seller had moved indoors. Mara walked the aisles looking for pears. At the far end, a young man had stacked green and russet ones in shallow wooden boxes.

“Are these local?” she asked.

“About forty miles away.” He picked one up. “These are ready today. The green ones need a little longer.”

She bought four. As he placed them in a bag, she considered asking whether a woman had sold pears here twenty years earlier. But she could already imagine his apologetic shrug. He might not have been born then. She thanked him and took the bag outside.

There was a bench near the entrance, in a patch of sunlight. Mara sat down and ate the ripest pear. Juice ran over her fingers, and she had to search her coat pockets for a tissue. The fruit was sweet and slightly gritty. She remembered her father cutting pears into thin slices because he disliked biting around the core. That memory had nothing to do with the market, but she was glad to have it.

On the bus home, she wrote on the map beneath his note: *Bought four. Ate one.* She hesitated, then added the date.

The cake box was gone, but the boy and his mother were still aboard. He had filled another page with buses. This time their wheels were smaller, and the passengers had bodies. He showed Mara the drawing as she passed.

“You fixed them,” she said.

He pointed to one of the buses. “That’s the new route.”

He had drawn it turning away from the bridge. Beside the road stood a small figure with a speech bubble. Inside it, in careful letters, he had written: *WAIT.*

Mara sat down and folded the map. At home, she put three pears in a bowl and returned the map to the drawer. She left it near the front, where she could find it again.
